A two-dimensional plot on a plane of the panel box

Source: R/layers-plot-plane.R
annotation_plot_3d.Rd

Draws the panel of a whole two-dimensional ggplot, every layer with its panel background and grid lines, on a plane of the 3D panel, such as a wall behind the data. The plot's x runs along the first axis of plane and its y along the second; the remaining axis is fixed at at, where Inf and -Inf place the plot on the box sides at the upper and lower end of that axis (0 when no other layer trains that axis). By default the plot keeps its own coordinates: its panel covers its x and y ranges on the two plane axes, so its data line up with the 3D layers that share those axes. extent places it elsewhere.

Usage

annotation_plot_3d(
  plot,
  plane = "xz",
  at = Inf,
  extent = NULL,
  route = c("vector", "raster"),
  resolution = 150,
  alpha = 1
)

Arguments

plot

A two-dimensional ggplot with a single panel.

plane

Two distinct axis letters: the axis carrying the plot's x then the axis carrying its y, for example "xz", "yz" or "xy".

at

Position on the remaining axis.

extent

NULL, or four numbers c(min, max, min, max): the positions of the plot's panel along the two plane axes. A reversed pair mirrors the plot.

route

"vector" or "raster" (which requires ragg).

resolution

Pixels along each side of the raster image.

alpha

Opacity multiplying the plot's own.

Value

A ggplot2 layer.

Details

The vector route decomposes the drawn panel into points, lines, polygons, rectangles and text that join the 3D scene and its exact visibility, as matplotlib places 2D artists on a plane of 3D axes and ggcube projects layers onto the faces of its cube. Marks lie in the plane, foreshortened with it, at the size they have on a 2D panel 4 inches wide; text faces the viewer and is drawn over the scene. The raster route renders the panel to an image of resolution pixels a side, as rayshader does for a whole ggplot, and lays its pixels on the plane as rectangles, joining runs of equal colour; it suits dense plots whose vector form would be large.

References

Hunter (2007). Matplotlib: a 2D graphics environment. Computing in Science & Engineering 9, 90-95. doi:10.1109/MCSE.2007.55

See also

facet_slices_3d() for small multiples on parallel planes.

Examples

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(200), y = rnorm(200))
d$z <- d$x * d$y + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)
side <- ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(x, z)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "grey40", size = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x)
ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  annotation_plot_3d(side, plane = "xz", at = Inf) +
  geom_point_3d(colour = "steelblue") +
  coord_3d()
